This is highly unlikely to be seen by a significant number of people given the current population, and the loud endorsement of bad safety but I am speaking out anyways. If you want to see how to start an electrical fire, go ask r/nerf for electric mods.

-

In terms of electric blaster modifications, there is one type of built-in safety, the thermistor. If too much current is put through the thermistor, its material composition will temporarily cut the circuit. This is commonly the first item removed.

-

When buying 14500 sized lithium batteries, do not buy the Trustfire and Ultrafire brands. They are low-current and have overstated capacity.

-

For full performance value, always replace stock wiring with 18 or 16 gauge stranded core wire. Even if you only use alkalines and Ni-MH rechargeables, 22 gauge stranded wire is only capable of carrying about 2 amps. Stock motors draw 3 amps or more.

For quick drop-in performance, a AA sized 14500 lithium manganese oxide (IMR) battery will suffice. The thermistor will likely have to be bypassed or removed.

Replacing the battery tray and tray connectors with a Ni-MH battery pack is acceptable and offers additional performance in case wire replacement is not enough.

Even more performance can be gained by a motor replacement.

-

There are four major types of rechargeable battery, nickel-metal hydride (Ni-MH), lithium manganese oxide (IMR), lithium polymer (LIPO), and lithium iron oxide.

In terms of damage potential during an accident, Ni-MH has the least damage potential, usually involving electrolyte leakage.

Lithium manganese oxide requires substantial abuse, and in most failures, will vent gas.

Lithium polymer is also relatively safe, being used in most modern smartphones, but is extremely prone to damage. In the case of a failure, lithium polymer will explode and possibly start a lithium fire, which cannot be extinguished with water.

Lithium iron oxide is a first generation type, and is extremely prone to failure. A lithium iron oxide battery can catch on fire merely by running low on capacity. This is the type of battery that caused incidents in Boeing 787s.

-

Do not, under any circumstances, use an electrical circuit without a safety cutoff paired with an extremely high current power source. This is less dangerous in the case of a Ni-MH battery since a vast majority of Ni-MH battery failures involve leakage.

If you choose to use a lithium polymer battery pack, always add a fuse to the circuit, as any failure in the battery pack will cause an explosion and fire. There is a reason the rc airplane hobbyists always carry a fire extinguisher.

The consensus for choice of batteries is lithium polymer. The reasoning given is that even if you use stock motors, they will draw 20 amps each during a stall, and any other battery type will be stressed and fail. This is the most dangerous bullshit you will find in the nerf community. When an electric motor stalls, it will have an extremely high power draw. If, however, your power source is actually capable of supporting stall power, and the stall is due to obstruction, the motor will fail quickly and catastrophically. Combine that with a lithium fire, and you've got performance nerfing.
